messages.author: daf017f67eba24e8
messages.subject: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
parts:
Before asking for advice let me say 2 quick things:

1) I'm fairly new to R and ggplot2, but I'm very excited about
ggplot2. Just using facet_grid has changed my life, not to mention
learning the grammar.

2) There was an older post enquiring about extending facet_grid (or
facet_wrap) beyond its current capabilities. (there were no replies).
I'm wondering about this too, but I'm also suspecting that if I were
clever enough, I might be able to get some of the functionality i'm
looking for. I didnt see any other older posts on this topic.

I'm using facet_grid to show the results for 3 different statistics
at, say, 4 levels of modeling resolution, that is stats~level. So the
grid is 4x3. Within each facet/subplot, there are 4 models on the x
axis and their score on the y. Furthermore, above each model tick
there are 4 jittered points with colors showing results for 4
different model setups. THat's awesome and easy in ggplot2!

All of the above conveniently summarizes data at 1 location. But I
have 6 locations, which is another faceting dimension, if you will.
But I find myself having exhausted facet_grid. Maybe I could do
something like facet_wrap(~(stats~level)) but I'm assuming that wont
work.

What I'm currently doing is using viewport and looping over the
data.frame, subsetting on location in each iteration and plotting to
the desired location in the multi-plot output. This actually works
well, and is kind of an adhoc facet_array or facet_matrix. The only
unsavory thing is the unnecessary repetition of the color legend. If
this were a true "facet_array" it would just plot that once in a
easily manageable way.

What I'm grappling with and looking for advice on is the best way to
banish the multiple color legends and efficiently get one legend in a
nice place while using viewport, or any other way that would work.


Thanks,

James

The natural syntax for this would by
~ stats + level

> What I'm currently doing is using viewport and looping over the

> banish the multiple color legends and efficiently get one legend in a
> nice place while using viewport, or any other way that would work.

You can disable the plotting of the legend by
opts(position.legend = "none")
and you can get a plot using only the legend by (for example)
opts(legend.position = "right", keep = "legend_box")
I don't remember if this leaves space for the "main" plot but doesn't
do it, or whether the viewport gets filled with the legend (the latter
would be preferred).

I had the same question a while back. Perhaps this solution should be
documented somewhere?

Kasper

messages.subject: Re: extension of facet_grid? facet_array? tricks?
parts:
Hi Kasper,

thanks, this is a step in the right direction. It appears that going
this route, so that the plot is laid out nicely, involves using
viewport in a detailed fashion. My first reading of viewport was
somewhat opaque, but I'll mess with it. If someone can illustrate a
proper way to do this with the code I've now provided below, I'd be
grateful.

Re the code below, there was a post which seems to have evaporated,
asking for some reproducible code. I shied away from this in my first
post, since it seemed like a lot of details, but I've now provided it
below. You should just be able to run it to see what i'm complaining
about, the repeated legends that I have to wrestle with. The second
plot, shows removal of all legends. I havent shown plotting only the
legend as Kaspar suggested, but it does omit the plot and put the
legend where it would have been with the plot present, at least using
the snytax of the previous post.

To me, resorting to witholding legends/plots and using view port is
less than ideal because its conjuring memories of some of the things I
hoped ggplot would cure. This is what I was alluding to when I wrote
the nonsense syntax facet_wrap(~(stats~level)) i wasnt being careful
here. More precisely, it should have been something more like
facet_grid(site~(stats~level)), since ggplot would need to know what
variables to be subsetting on at each level. This is essentially what
I have achieved by doing the subsetting in the loop (over ss below),
only I'm forced to fuss with legends which is so un-ggplot2. To me it
makes sense to want to extend the idea of facet_grid to more
dimensions. I think some could argue for using the formula syntax to
get at some of this, but i havent been sucessful with this and it
seems like it would tend to clutter more than simplify the
presentation.

cheers,
James

---------------------------------------
require(ggplot2)

#set up the data frame
len=243 #=3^5
data=data.frame(value=rnorm(len))
data$setup=factor( c(rep('setup1',len/3),rep('setup2',len/3),rep
('setup3',len/3)) )
data$site=factor( rep (c(rep('site1',len/9),rep('site2',len/9),rep
('site3',len/9)), 3) )
data$level=factor( rep( c(rep('lev1',len/27),rep('lev2',len/27),rep
('lev3',len/27)),9 ))
data$model=factor( rep( c(rep('mod1',len/81),rep('mod2',len/81),rep
('mod3',len/81)),27 ))
data$stat=factor( rep( c('stat1','stat2','stat3'),81 ) )

# will need this for subsetting
sites=unique(data$site)

# need this for viewporting
vplayout<-function(x,y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x,layout.pos.col=y)

#some plot option values
grid.line.type='solid'
grid.line.size=.2
model.name.size=6

# first plot, showing multiple, repeated, unnecessary legends
x11(h=6,w=15)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,3)))
for (ss in 1:length(sites)) {
site=sites[ss]
plot <-
ggplot( data[which(data$site==site),],
aes(model,value,shape=setup)) +
geom_jitter()+
facet_grid(level~stat)+
theme_bw() +
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text
(size=model.name.size,hjust=1,angle=90),
panel.grid.major= theme_line
(linetype=grid.line.type,
colour='gray50',size=grid.line.size),
title=site)
print(plot , vp=vplayout(((ss-1) %/% 3)+1,((ss-1) %% 3)+1))
}

## this is removing the legends, all of them....
x11(h=6,w=15)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,3)))
for (ss in 1:length(sites)) {
site=sites[ss]
plot <-
ggplot( data[which(data$site==site),],
aes(model,value,shape=setup)) +
geom_jitter()+
facet_grid(level~stat) +
theme_bw() +
opts(axis.text.x=theme_text
(size=model.name.size,hjust=1,angle=90),
panel.grid.major= theme_line
(linetype=grid.line.type,
colour='gray50',size=grid.line.size),
title=site,
legend.position='none')
print(plot , vp=vplayout(((ss-1) %/% 3)+1,((ss-1) %% 3)+1))
}

parts:
Hi James,

I agree that it's frustrating to have to do it yourself for more
complicated facetting examples like the attached. However, it's very
difficult to design a system that works more generally. For example,
how would your proposed syntax work if you wanted facet_wrap nested
inside facet_grid? Should you allow a fixed amount of nesting, or an
unlimited amount, so you could have facet_wrap nested inside
facet_grid nested inside facet_wrap? How would you deal with free
scales? To start with, what sorts of restrictions would you even want
to apply? If you wanted manually specified limits that vary across
facets, how would you describe them? (I haven't even figured out how
to do this for the simpler cases that currently exist).

Then once you've figured out the basic syntax and structure, you have
to write all the drawing code, dealing with the various possibilities
for axis positions. And then you have to document it all. It's a lot
of work for a feature that will only be used by a few people,
especially when there is already a way to work around it.

That's not to say I'd never implement it, because I like the elegance
of having a fully recursive facetting specification, but it's pretty
unlikely unless I have some insight into a nice way to represent all
the possibilities.

Hadley

On Nov 19, 6:29 pm, McCreight <mccre...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Re the code below, there was a post which seems to have evaporated,

Yeah, I used the "Reply to author" option in Google groups. Nice to
hear that you got it; I never see those messages again myself 8-)

> asking for some reproducible code. I shied away from this in my first
> post, since it seemed like a lot of details, but I've now provided it
> below.

Thanks! If I understand correctly, this gives what you want except for
splitting on "site":
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~stat)

or for the hardcore ggplotter:
ggplot(data, aes(model, value, shape=setup)) + facet_grid(level~stat)
+ geom_point()

(or you could use colour=setup to match the image you posted
here...mind the u, "color" won't work as of ggplot2 0.8.3)).

I _think_ you're supposed to be able to use facets=level~site+stat:
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~site+stat)

However, the corresponding example (search for ". ~ vs + am") at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/facet_grid.html
is currently broken. (Faceting on multiple row (or column) variables
is also described in the "facet grid" section of the "positioning"
chapter of the ggplot2 book, so I guess it _is_ intended to work.)

A crude workaround is
data$sitestat <- with(data, interaction(site, stat))
qplot(data=data, model, value, shape=setup, facets=level~sitestat)

This gives you a quick overview, though with clumsy column headers and
without nice gaps between sites. On the other hand, if I needed a plot
for publication now, I'd just loop over levels of "site", make
separate plots, crop away the unnecessary legends, and combine the
plots outside of R. Hopefully, faceting on multiple row (or column)
variables will be fixed in a future version.

Hope this helps,
Jon Olav

How about two options:
* a table with faceting variables plus columns xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax?
lim <- ddply(mpg, ~drv+cyl, .fun=function(d) with(d, c(range(cty),
range(hwy))))
drv cyl V1 V2 V3 V4
1 4 4 15 21 20 28
2 4 6 13 17 17 25
[...]
* a function taking the faceting variables as input and returning c
(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) as output?
limfun <- function(...) merge(lim, data.frame(...))
facets <- data.frame(drv=c("f", "r"), cyl=c(4, 8))
limfun(facets)
drv cyl V1 V2 V3 V4
1 f 4 18 35 24 44
2 r 8 11 16 15 26

maybe a good workaround could be a more flexible way to arrange
several ggplots in a page. For example, latticeExtra provides a
c.trellis method whereby two plots can be combined into one with some
parameters in common (e.g. one axis, the legend, etc.).

This requires full control over the size of the different viewports of
ggplot (making sure the panels are aligned and have the same size),
which I don't think we have at the moment. I imagine the following
typical example,


p1 = qplot(...)
p2 = qplot(...)

p12 = arrange(p1, p2, ncol=2, common.yaxis = FALSE,
                    common.legend=TRUE, legend.position="right")

This could obviously become more complicated when the plots have
facets (do we try to align all the panels? -- probably not), but at
least some of the options could remain available (legend, layout,
title, theme, etc.).

The main problem with implementing this currently is that if you
remove an element of a ggplot, such as the legend, it resizes itself
to fill the viewport. Also, if you want to plot only a legend, its
size is rather bizarre (e.g. I failed in calculating its grobWidth in
absolute units), which makes it difficult to control the layout of
several plots accurately.


Just a thought anyway,
